2027-02-02.title: Fifth Tuesday of Denha · Mayaltho: The Presentation of the Lord in the Temple
2027-02-02.readTitle: Readings of the day (First Set; mapped from the official calendar, verify locally)
readings: The Servant, a light to the nations
Christ, the end of the law
The Presentation of the Lord in the Temple
2027-02-02.alt: Season of Denha. Mayaltho, the feast of the Presentation of the Lord in the Temple. World Day for Consecrated Life. Weekday readings of the day: 1 Corinthians 15:20–28; Matthew 24:37–44.
2027-02-02.verse: for my eyes have seen your salvation, which you have prepared in the presence of all peoples, a light for revelation to the Gentiles and for glory to your people Israel.
theo: Forty days after his birth the Lord enters his Temple. The Church of the East calls this feast Mayaltho, the Entrance: the child carried in Mary's arms is the Lord of the Temple coming into his own house. The first reading shows the law the Holy Family obeyed. After the birth of a son a mother waited forty days for her purification, and then brought “a lamb in its first year for a burnt offering, and a pigeon or a turtledove for a sin offering.” The law made room for the poor: “If she cannot afford a sheep, she shall take two turtledoves or two pigeons.” Luke tells us that Mary and Joseph offered “a pair of turtledoves or two young pigeons.” They were poor. They also fulfilled another law, that every firstborn son belongs to God: “Every firstborn male shall be designated as holy to the Lord.” The true Lamb was carried into the Temple, and the poor man's offering was made for him.

Two old people were waiting. Simeon was “righteous and devout, looking forward to the consolation of Israel, and the Holy Spirit rested on him.” Guided by the Spirit he came into the Temple at the very moment the parents brought the child in. He took the child in his arms and praised God: “Master, now you are dismissing your servant in peace, according to your word; for my eyes have seen your salvation, which you have prepared in the presence of all peoples, a light for revelation to the Gentiles and for glory to your people Israel.” Then he turned to the mother with a harder word: “This child is destined for the falling and the rising of many in Israel, and to be a sign that will be opposed”, and a sword would pierce her own soul too. Anna, a widow of eighty-four, “never left the temple but worshiped there with fasting and prayer night and day.” She too began to praise God and to speak about the child “to all who were looking for the redemption of Jerusalem.” The prophet Malachi had promised that “the Lord whom you seek will suddenly come to his temple.” He came quietly, as a baby, and only those who were waiting recognized him.

Isaiah describes the one Simeon held: “Here is my servant, whom I uphold, my chosen, in whom my soul delights.” He will not shout or crush the weak: “a bruised reed he will not break, and a dimly burning wick he will not quench.” God gives him “as a covenant to the people, a light to the nations, to open the eyes that are blind.” Simeon's song repeats this promise: a light for the Gentiles, and so for us in India too. Paul, in the Epistle, carries the sorrow of the sword. He grieves that many of his own people stumbled over “the stumbling stone”, and he prays that they may be saved. Yet he states the meaning of this feast in one line: “For Christ is the end of the law so that there may be righteousness for everyone who believes.” The child who was presented according to the law is the goal toward which the whole law was moving.

The weekday readings keep the Denha light turned toward the end of time. Paul proclaims that “as all die in Adam, so all will be made alive in Christ”, and Jesus warns, “Keep awake therefore, for you do not know on what day your Lord is coming.” Simeon and Anna kept awake for a lifetime, and their eyes saw salvation. Today is also the World Day for Consecrated Life. Religious sisters, brothers and priests, so many of them from our own families, are presented to God like the child in the Temple, poor, chaste and obedient, so that the light of Christ may reach every people.
conn: Mayaltho.
A Syriac name meaning the Entrance: the Lord enters his Temple. The Greek Churches call the feast the Meeting (Hypapante), the meeting of the Lord with his people in Simeon and Anna.
Forty days.
Leviticus 12:2–4: forty days after the birth of a son. The feast falls forty days after Christmas.
The offering of the poor.
Leviticus 12:8 allowed two birds instead of a lamb; Luke 2:24 shows that the Holy Family made the offering of the poor.
The firstborn.
Exodus 13:2, 12–15: every firstborn son belongs to the Lord, in memory of the Passover. Jesus, the firstborn of all creation, is wholly the Father's.
The Lord comes to his temple.
Malachi 3:1 is fulfilled quietly: the Lord of the Temple enters it carried by his mother.
The stone and the sign.
Romans 9:33 joins Isaiah 28:16 and 8:14; Simeon's sign that will be opposed (Luke 2:34) is the same stone, on which some stumble and others build.
Simeon's song.
Luke 2:29–32, called the Nunc Dimittis from its first Latin words, has been prayed by Christians at the close of day for many centuries.
The weekday readings.
1 Corinthians 15:20–28 and Matthew 24:37–44: Christ the first fruits of the resurrection, and the call to keep awake, which Simeon and Anna kept.
altar: Simeon took the child in his arms; in the Holy Qurbana the priest takes the same Lord in his hands and lifts him up, and we receive him as Simeon did.
The Lord who entered his Temple enters our churches and our hearts at every Qurbana. Like Simeon we can say after Communion: my eyes have seen your salvation.
outline: Opening
Ask: for what have you waited longest in your life?
Point 1 · Presented to the Lord
Forty days, two birds, the firstborn.
Point 2 · A light to the nations
The Servant who does not break the bruised reed.
Point 3 · A sign that will be opposed
The stone of stumbling and the sword in Mary's heart.
Point 4 · Fasting and prayer night and day
Anna and Simeon, who kept awake.
Closing image
An old man holding a baby in the Temple, his face full of light.
Take-home line
“My eyes have seen your salvation.”
live: Present yourself (Luke 2:22)
Begin each day this week by offering yourself, your family and your work to God.
Pray for consecrated persons
Pray by name for a religious sister, brother or priest from your family or parish, and send them a word of thanks.
Be patient like Simeon
Keep waiting in prayer for one intention you have almost given up on.
Bring light
Visit or call an elderly person who prays for the Church, as Anna did.
fathers: Let us all hasten to meet Christ, carrying lights: the true light has come into the world, and like Simeon we receive him in our arms and are filled with his brightness.
Whoever wishes to be released in peace must come to the Temple, wait for the Lord's Anointed, and take the Word of God into the arms of faith.
magis: Catechism 529
The Presentation shows Jesus as the firstborn Son who belongs to the Lord; Simeon and Anna stand for Israel's expectation meeting its Saviour.
Catechism 583
It was in the Temple that Joseph and Mary presented him forty days after his birth.
Lumen Gentium 57
Mary heard Simeon foretell that her Son would be a sign of contradiction and that a sword would pierce her soul.
Catechism 1953
Christ is the end of the law: in him the moral law finds its fullness.
Vita consecrata 1
The consecrated life is a gift of God the Father to his Church through the Holy Spirit.
saints: The righteous old man and the prophetess of the tribe of Asher who recognized the child in the Temple; the Eastern Churches honour them on the days around this feast.
2027-02-02.prayer: Lord Jesus Christ, firstborn Son of the Father, you were carried into your Temple and offered with the gift of the poor. Let us, like Simeon, take you into our arms with faith, and like Anna, wait for you with fasting and prayer. Shine on all the nations as the light of revelation, strengthen your mother's children when the sword pierces their hearts, and bless all who have consecrated their lives to you. Glory to you, with the Father and the Holy Spirit, for ever. Amen.

2027-02-07.title: First Sunday of the Great Fast
2027-02-07.readTitle: Readings of the day (First Set; mapped from the official calendar, verify locally)
readings: Put away the old self and clothe yourselves with the new
2027-02-07.alt: Season of the Great Fast (Sauma Ramba). Pethurtha: on the threshold of the fast, families are reconciled and share a last festive meal; the Great Fast begins tomorrow, Monday 8 February, a day of fasting and abstinence, and in many parishes ashes are blessed. Longer forms in the calendar: Exodus 34:1–7, 27–35; Isaiah 58:1–12, 14; Ephesians 4:17–5:4, 15–21; Matthew 3:16–4:11.
2027-02-07.verse: One does not live by bread alone, but by every word that comes from the mouth of God.
theo: With this Sunday the Church enters the Great Fast, the fifty days that lead to the Pasha of the Lord. The first reading shows what a fast is for. Moses goes up Sinai to receive the covenant again after Israel's sin with the golden calf: “He was there with the LORD forty days and forty nights; he neither ate bread nor drank water. And he wrote on the tablets the words of the covenant, the ten commandments.” When he comes down, “Moses did not know that the skin of his face shone because he had been talking with God.” The people are afraid to come near, so he covers his face with a veil, taking it off only when he goes in to speak with the LORD. Fasting is not first of all about food. It is about being with God so long and so closely that something of his light begins to shine in us, often without our knowing it.

Isaiah warns that a fast can also be empty. The people complain: “Why do we fast, but you do not see? Why humble ourselves, but you do not notice?” God answers: “Look, you serve your own interest on your fast day, and oppress all your workers. Look, you fast only to quarrel and to fight.” Then he describes the fast he wants: “Is not this the fast that I choose: to loose the bonds of injustice, to undo the thongs of the yoke, to let the oppressed go free, and to break every yoke? Is it not to share your bread with the hungry, and bring the homeless poor into your house; when you see the naked, to cover them, and not to hide yourself from your own kin?” Only then: “your light shall break forth like the dawn, and your healing shall spring up quickly.” Paul gives the same programme in the language of clothing. We are to put away “your old self, corrupt and deluded by its lusts, and to be renewed in the spirit of your minds, and to clothe yourselves with the new self, created according to the likeness of God in true righteousness and holiness.” The Great Fast is a change of clothes: the old self off, Christ on.

In the Gospel, “Jesus was led up by the Spirit into the wilderness to be tempted by the devil. He fasted forty days and forty nights, and afterwards he was famished.” The tempter comes three times. Turn stones into bread: use your power for your own hunger. Throw yourself down from the temple: force God to prove his care with a spectacle. Fall down and worship me: take the kingdoms of the world by the easy road. Each time Jesus answers with the word of God from Deuteronomy, the book of Israel's forty years in the desert: “One does not live by bread alone, but by every word that comes from the mouth of God”; “Do not put the Lord your God to the test”; “Worship the Lord your God, and serve only him.” Where Adam failed in the garden and Israel failed in the desert, the new Adam stands firm, and “suddenly angels came and waited on him.” We do not fast alone. We fast in him, and his victory becomes ours. So tonight, at Pethurtha, let families forgive one another, and tomorrow let us begin the fifty days with prayer, fasting and almsgiving, so that our faces too may shine with the light of the Risen One at Easter.
conn: Forty days.
Moses on Sinai (Exodus 34:28), Elijah walking to Horeb (1 Kings 19:8), Israel's forty years (Deuteronomy 8:2), and Jesus in the wilderness: forty is the time of testing and of meeting God.
The shining face.
Paul sees in Moses' veil a sign of the old covenant; in Christ “all of us, with unveiled faces”, are transformed into his image (2 Corinthians 3:7–18).
Fasting and almsgiving.
Isaiah 58 joins fasting to justice and sharing bread; Tobit 12:8 and Matthew 6:1–18 join prayer, fasting and almsgiving as the three works of the fast.
Three answers from Deuteronomy.
Deuteronomy 8:3; 6:16; 6:13: Jesus relives Israel's desert test and remains faithful where Israel failed.
The new Adam.
Adam was tempted with food in a garden of plenty and fell; Christ was tempted with food in a desert of hunger and stood firm (Romans 5:19).
Pethurtha.
The Sunday evening on the threshold of the Great Fast, kept in Syro-Malabar families as a time of reconciliation and a simple farewell to festive food before the fifty days.
altar: The bread Jesus refused to make from stones he now gives us freely: himself, the Bread of life, the word that comes from the mouth of God made food.
During the Great Fast the Holy Qurbana is not a break from the fast but its heart: we fast in order to hunger more deeply for him.
outline: Opening
Ask: what do you plan to give up this Great Fast, and why?
Point 1 · Forty days with God
Moses' shining face.
Point 2 · Not by bread alone
The three temptations and the word of God.
Point 3 · The fast that I choose
Justice, sharing bread, and light breaking forth.
Point 4 · Put on the new self
Renewed in the spirit of your minds.
Closing image
Moses coming down the mountain, his face shining, not knowing it.
Take-home line
“One does not live by bread alone, but by every word that comes from the mouth of God.”
live: Be reconciled tonight
At Pethurtha, ask pardon of one family member and forgive one person from your heart.
Fast with the word (Matthew 4:4)
Read one chapter of a Gospel every day of the Great Fast.
Share your bread (Isaiah 58:7)
Set aside what you save by fasting in a box, and give it to the poor at Easter.
Fast with your tongue
Give up gossip, harsh words and complaining, not only food.
fathers: Christ was tempted so that we might overcome: in him you were tempted, and in him you conquer. He took our flesh, so that his victory might be ours.
Do you fast? Prove it by your works. If you see a poor person, have pity; if an enemy, be reconciled. Let not only the mouth fast, but also the eyes, the ears, the hands and the feet.
magis: Catechism 538–540
Jesus' temptation in the desert: the new Adam remains faithful where the first Adam gave in.
Catechism 1434
Interior penance is expressed above all in fasting, prayer and almsgiving.
Catechism 1438
The seasons and days of penance, especially the forty days, are intense moments of the Church's penitential practice.
Catechism 2043
The precept of the Church on fasting and abstinence prepares us for the liturgical feasts.
Code of Canons of the Eastern Churches, can. 882
On days of penance the faithful keep fast or abstinence as determined by the particular law of their Church sui iuris.
saints: 8 Feb: the Great Fast begins (day of fasting and abstinence). 11 Feb: Our Lady of Lourdes, World Day of the Sick.
2027-02-07.prayer: Lord Jesus Christ, you fasted forty days in the wilderness and overcame the tempter by the word of God. As we begin the Great Fast, give us hunger for every word that comes from the mouth of God; let our fasting loose the bonds of injustice and share our bread with the hungry; strip away our old self and clothe us with the new; and keep us faithful to worship the Father alone, so that at your Resurrection our faces may shine with your light. Glory to you, with the Father and the Holy Spirit, for ever. Amen.

2027-02-14.title: Second Sunday of the Great Fast
2027-02-14.readTitle: Readings of the day (First Set; mapped from the official calendar, verify locally)
readings: Through the Jordan into the land of salvation
Not under law but under grace
2027-02-14.alt: Season of the Great Fast (Sauma Ramba). Sts Cyril and Methodius are honoured today in the Latin calendar.
2027-02-14.verse: “Everyone then who hears these words of mine and acts on them will be like a wise man who built his house on rock.
theo: The first reading sounds at first like a list of names and numbers, with one refrain tolling like a bell: “Thus all the days of Jared were nine hundred sixty-two years; and he died.” Methuselah lives longest of all, nine hundred sixty-nine years, “and he died.” One name breaks the pattern. “Enoch walked with God; then he was no more, because God took him.” He did not walk with God in a desert or a monastery: he “walked with God after the birth of Methuselah three hundred years, and had other sons and daughters.” His holiness was lived in an ordinary household. Sirach calls him “an example of repentance to all generations”, and Hebrews says that “he had pleased God.” At the end of the passage Lamech names his son Noah, saying, “Out of the ground that the LORD has cursed this one shall bring us relief from our work and from the toil of our hands.” Even under the long shadow of death God keeps hope alive. In this second week the Great Fast shows its real goal: not a list of things given up, but a life that walks with God.

In the second reading the priests carrying the ark come up out of the Jordan, and as soon as their feet touch dry ground the river returns and overflows its banks as before. Israel camps at Gilgal, and Joshua sets up the twelve stones taken from the riverbed. He gives the reason: “When your children ask their parents in time to come, ‘What do these stones mean?’ then you shall let your children know, ‘Israel crossed over the Jordan here on dry ground.’” The stones exist so that the story will be told, “so that all the peoples of the earth may know that the hand of the LORD is mighty.” Our Lenten customs are stones of this kind: the ash of the Vibhoodi, the abstinence kept by the whole house, the Way of the Cross on Fridays, the Puthen Pana sung in the evenings. When a child asks why we do not eat fish now, the answer is the story of Christ. Paul tells the baptised that they too have crossed a river. Everyone serves someone: “you are slaves of the one whom you obey, either of sin, which leads to death, or of obedience, which leads to righteousness.” “But now that you have been freed from sin and enslaved to God, the advantage you get is sanctification. The end is eternal life.” Then comes the great contrast between what we earn and what we are given: “For the wages of sin is death, but the free gift of God is eternal life in Christ Jesus our Lord.”

The Gospel is the ending of the Sermon on the Mount, and it is sobering: “Not everyone who says to me, ‘Lord, Lord,’ will enter the kingdom of heaven, but only the one who does the will of my Father in heaven.” Some will claim to have prophesied, cast out demons and done mighty works in his name, and he will answer, “I never knew you.” Then Jesus tells of two builders. The same rain falls on both houses, the same floods come, the same winds beat against them. The only difference is the foundation. The house of the one who hears and acts “did not fall, because it had been founded on rock”; the house of the one who hears and does not act falls, “and great was its fall!” Kerala knows what floods do to houses. The storms of illness, loss and temptation come to every home; what we build on is decided before they arrive. The Great Fast is digging time: hearing the word and doing it, until our life rests on Christ the rock. Today the Latin Church also honours Sts Cyril and Methodius, the brothers who gave the Slav peoples the Scriptures and the liturgy in their own language, so that the word might be both heard and lived.
conn: Enoch, an example of repentance.
Sirach 44:16 calls Enoch “an example of repentance to all generations”; Hebrews 11:5 says that by faith he was taken, because he had pleased God.
Noah, who brings relief.
Lamech's hope for his son (Genesis 5:29) leads to the flood and the ark; 1 Peter 3:20–21 sees the ark as a figure of baptism.
Gilgal.
The twelve stones stood at Gilgal, where Israel was circumcised and kept the Passover on entering the land (Joshua 5:2–10).
Through the Jordan.

Jesus was baptised in the Jordan (Matthew 3:13–17). The Fathers read Israel's crossing as a figure of baptism, and the Great Fast was the ancient season in which catechumens prepared for baptism at Easter.
Slaves of God.
Paul calls himself a servant, literally a slave, of Christ Jesus (Romans 1:1). Christian freedom is not doing whatever we please but belonging to the One who sets us free (Galatians 5:1, 13).
The rock.
God is Israel's rock (Psalm 18:2); Paul says “the rock was Christ” (1 Corinthians 10:4), and Jesus builds his Church on the rock of Peter (Matthew 16:18).
altar: At the Holy Qurbana we hear Christ's words and receive Christ himself; at the end we are sent out to do what we have heard, so that our house may stand on the rock.
Israel remembered the crossing with stones; Christ left us a living memorial, his Body and Blood, so that every generation may ask what it means and receive the answer.
outline: Opening
Ask: what is your life built on, and how do you know?
Point 1 · Walking with God
Enoch, holiness in an ordinary home.
Point 2 · What do these stones mean?
Our Lenten customs tell Christ's story to our children.
Point 3 · Wages and gift
Slaves of sin or servants of God.
Point 4 · Built on rock
Hearing and doing in the time of the fast.
Closing image
Twelve stones on the bank of a river, and a house standing after the flood.
Take-home line
“Everyone then who hears these words of mine and acts on them will be like a wise man who built his house on rock.”
live: Walk with God (Genesis 5:24)
Take a fifteen-minute walk each day this week and spend it in prayer, as Enoch walked with God.
Explain the stones (Joshua 4:21–22)
Tell your children or grandchildren this week why we keep the Great Fast, and what each custom means.
Choose the gift (Romans 6:23)
Make your Lenten confession before the third Sunday of the Great Fast.
Do one word (Matthew 7:24)
Choose one teaching from the Sermon on the Mount and put it into practice every day this week.
fathers: The rock is Christ. Whoever hears his words and does them builds on the rock; whoever only listens, however long and however gladly, builds on sand.
Do you fast? Show it by your works. If you see a poor person, take pity; if you see an enemy, be reconciled. Let not only the mouth fast, but the eyes, the ears, the hands and the feet.
magis: Catechism 2569
In the first chapters of Genesis prayer is lived as walking with God, as Enoch did.
Catechism 1434
Interior penance is expressed above all in fasting, prayer and almsgiving.
Catechism 1987–1992
Justification is the free gift of God's grace, received in faith and baptism, which frees us from sin and makes us servants of righteousness.
Catechism 2826
We enter the kingdom of heaven not by saying “Lord, Lord” but by doing the will of the Father.
Code of Canons of the Eastern Churches, canon 882
On days of penance the faithful observe fasting or abstinence as the particular law of their own Church determines.
saints: 15–20 Feb: second week of the Great Fast. 19 Feb: Second Friday of the Great Fast (abstinence; Way of the Cross).
2027-02-14.prayer: Lord Jesus Christ, rock of our salvation, you brought us through the waters of baptism into the land of your grace. Teach us to walk with God like Enoch, to tell our children what our Lenten stones mean, and to choose the free gift of eternal life rather than the wages of sin. Let us not only call you Lord, but do the will of your Father, so that our house may stand when the storms come. Glory to you, with the Father and the Holy Spirit, for ever. Amen.

2027-02-01.title: Fifth Monday of Denha
2027-02-01.readTitle: Readings of the day (First Set; mapped from the official calendar, verify locally)
readings: Your faith has made you well
2027-02-01.alt: Season of Denha. Tomorrow, 2 February, is Mayaltho, the Presentation of the Lord in the Temple.
2027-02-01.verse: But the Lord is faithful; he will strengthen you and guard you from the evil one.
theo: Paul ends his letter to the Thessalonians by asking for their prayers: “pray for us, so that the word of the Lord may spread rapidly and be glorified everywhere, just as it is among you, and that we may be rescued from wicked and evil people; for not all have faith.” He is honest about the opposition he meets. But he does not rest his hope on how many believe. He rests it on someone else: “But the Lord is faithful; he will strengthen you and guard you from the evil one.” Our faith rises and falls; the Lord's faithfulness does not. So Paul can end with a blessing that is also a direction for the whole of life: “May the Lord direct your hearts to the love of God and to the steadfastness of Christ.”

In the Gospel two daughters meet the faithful Lord. A leader of the synagogue kneels before Jesus: “My daughter has just died; but come and lay your hand on her, and she will live.” On the way a woman who has suffered from hemorrhages for twelve years comes up behind him. Under the law her illness made her unclean and kept her apart from worship and from people. She does not dare to ask; she only reaches out: “If I only touch his cloak, I will be made well.” Jesus turns and looks at her. He does not scold her for touching him; he calls her by a family name: “Take heart, daughter; your faith has made you well.” Then at the leader's house, among the flute players and the noisy mourners, he says, “Go away; for the girl is not dead but sleeping.” They laugh at him. He goes in, takes her by the hand, and the girl gets up. In these last days of Denha Christ is revealed as Lord over sickness and death. A touch of faith is enough, because the one who is touched is faithful.
outline: Opening
Ask: when your faith is small, on whose faithfulness do you lean?
Point 1 · The Lord is faithful
Our faith wavers; his does not.
Point 2 · If I only touch his cloak
The woman who reached out; take heart, daughter.
Point 3 · Not dead but sleeping
He takes the girl by the hand.
Take-home line
“But the Lord is faithful.”
live: Pray for the spread of the word (2 Thessalonians 3:1)
Pray today for a missionary, a catechist or a preacher you know by name.
Reach out and touch
Bring one long-standing trouble to Jesus in a short, trusting prayer, as the woman did.
2027-02-01.prayer: Lord Jesus Christ, faithful and true, you turned to the woman who touched your cloak and took the dead girl by the hand. Strengthen us and guard us from the evil one, direct our hearts to the love of God and to your own steadfastness, and when our faith is small, let it be enough to reach out and touch you. Amen.
altar: At the Holy Qurbana we do more than touch the fringe of his cloak: he gives himself into our hands and into our hearts.

2027-02-03.title: Fifth Wednesday of Denha
2027-02-03.readTitle: Readings of the day (First Set; mapped from the official calendar, verify locally)
readings: My food is to do the will of him who sent me
2027-02-03.alt: Season of Denha. St Blaise, bishop and martyr, is also remembered today.
2027-02-03.verse: My food is to do the will of him who sent me and to complete his work.
theo: Paul writes to Timothy as an old man near the end of his race, and his words have the weight of a last will: “I solemnly urge you: proclaim the message; be persistent whether the time is favorable or unfavorable; convince, rebuke, and encourage, with the utmost patience in teaching.” He knows what is coming: “the time is coming when people will not put up with sound doctrine, but having itching ears, they will accumulate for themselves teachers to suit their own desires.” Our age of endless voices, each telling us what we like to hear, is not new. Timothy must stay steady: “always be sober, endure suffering, do the work of an evangelist, carry out your ministry fully.” And Paul himself is ready to give the last drop: “As for me, I am already being poured out as a libation, and the time of my departure has come.”

In the Gospel the Samaritan woman has just met Jesus at the well. The disciples come back and are astonished that he is speaking with a woman. She, meanwhile, “left her water jar and went back to the city.” The jar she came for is forgotten; she has found living water. She says to the people, “Come and see a man who told me everything I have ever done! He cannot be the Messiah, can he?” The disciples urge Jesus, “Rabbi, eat something,” and he answers, “I have food to eat that you do not know about.” They think someone has brought him lunch. He explains: “My food is to do the will of him who sent me and to complete his work.” Then he points to the Samaritans already walking toward him across the fields: “look around you, and see how the fields are ripe for harvesting.” One sows and another reaps. In Denha Christ is revealed even to the Samaritans, the outsiders, through a woman who simply said: come and see. We in Kerala reap what the apostle Thomas and many generations of priests, religious and catechists sowed. “Others have labored, and you have entered into their labor.”
outline: Opening
Ask: what really feeds you, what gives you strength to go on?
Point 1 · Proclaim the message
In season and out of season; itching ears.
Point 2 · She left her water jar
Come and see a man who told me everything.
Point 3 · My food is to do his will
The fields are ripe; others have laboured.
Take-home line
“My food is to do the will of him who sent me.”
live: Leave a water jar
Name one thing you cling to that keeps you from Christ, and set it down for a day.
Thank those who sowed (John 4:38)
Thank God by name for the person who first taught you the faith, and pray for them.
2027-02-03.prayer: Lord Jesus, at the well you gave living water to a woman who came only for water, and she ran to bring others to you. Make your Father's will our food, give us courage to proclaim your word in every season, and let us gather with joy the harvest that others have sown. Amen.
altar: At the altar Christ gives us the food we do not know about: his own Body and Blood, so that we may do the Father's will and complete his work.

2027-02-04.title: Fifth Thursday of Denha · St John de Britto
2027-02-04.readTitle: Readings of the day (First Set; mapped from the official calendar, verify locally)
readings: Regard the patience of our Lord as salvation
Do not judge, and you will not be judged
2027-02-04.alt: Season of Denha. St John de Britto, martyr: 1 Corinthians 9:19–23; John 15:18–25.
2027-02-04.verse: Do not judge, and you will not be judged; do not condemn, and you will not be condemned. Forgive, and you will be forgiven;
theo: Peter's second letter closes with a word about time. Christians were asking why the Lord delayed his coming. Peter answers: “regard the patience of our Lord as salvation.” Every day God waits is a day of mercy, given so that more may repent. He warns that some twist the hard things in Paul's letters “to their own destruction”, and he ends with a simple programme: “grow in the grace and knowledge of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ.” In the Gospel Jesus asks us to treat others as God treats us: “Do not judge, and you will not be judged; do not condemn, and you will not be condemned. Forgive, and you will be forgiven; give, and it will be given to you. A good measure, pressed down, shaken together, running over, will be put into your lap.” Then comes the picture that makes us smile and then makes us blush: “Why do you see the speck in your neighbor's eye, but do not notice the log in your own eye?” The patience God shows us is the measure of the patience we owe to others. Only the one who has first removed his own log can help a brother with his speck.

Today the Church honours St John de Britto, a Portuguese Jesuit martyred in Tamil Nadu. Born in Lisbon in 1647 and brought up at the royal court, he left everything to serve in the Madurai mission. There he lived as an Indian ascetic, a pandaraswami, in saffron dress, eating simple vegetarian food, speaking Tamil, so that the people knew him as Arul Anandar. He lived Paul's words in the saint's readings: “I have become all things to all people, that I might by all means save some.” He was arrested, tortured and expelled, went back to Portugal, refused the comfortable life offered to him there, and returned to the Marava country. When a local prince, Thadiya Thevar, was baptized and kept only one wife as the Gospel requires, the family of a dismissed wife complained to the ruler, and the missionary was condemned. He was beheaded at Oriyur on 4 February 1693, and Pope Pius XII canonized him in 1947. He had heard the Lord's warning: “If the world hates you, be aware that it hated me before it hated you.” He judged no one; he gave himself, good measure, running over.
outline: Opening
Ask: whose speck do you notice most easily?
Point 1 · The patience of our Lord
Every day of waiting is a day of mercy.
Point 2 · Do not judge
The good measure, pressed down, running over.
Point 3 · The log in my own eye
First take out your own log.
Point 4 · All things to all people
St John de Britto, Arul Anandar.
Take-home line
“Forgive, and you will be forgiven.”
live: Look for the log (Luke 6:41)
Before you criticize anyone today, name one fault of your own and ask God's pardon for it.
Pray for missionaries
Pray for missionaries in North India and elsewhere who live among people of other cultures, as Arul Anandar did.
2027-02-04.prayer: Lord Jesus Christ, you are patient with us, not wanting any to perish. Free us from judging and condemning, teach us to forgive and to give in good measure, take the log out of our own eyes, and through the prayers of St John de Britto make us all things to all people, so that we may win some for you. Amen.
altar: At the Holy Qurbana we receive mercy pressed down and running over: the Lord gives himself to sinners who have not earned him.

2027-02-05.title: Fifth Friday of Denha · Commemoration of All the Faithful Departed
2027-02-05.readTitle: Readings of the day (First Set; mapped from the official calendar, verify locally)
readings: Just as you did it to one of the least of these
2027-02-05.alt: Season of Denha. On this last Friday of Denha, just before the Great Fast, the Church remembers all the faithful departed. Longer forms in the calendar: Sirach 44:1–45:6; 1 Corinthians 15:34–57; Matthew 25:31–46.
2027-02-05.verse: It is sown in dishonor, it is raised in glory. It is sown in weakness, it is raised in power.
theo: On the Fridays of Denha the Church remembers those through whom Christ was made visible. On this last Friday, before the Great Fast begins, she remembers all the faithful departed, so that we enter the fast in communion with the whole family of God, living and dead. Ezekiel stands in a valley full of bones, “and they were very dry.” God asks him, “Mortal, can these bones live?” The prophet gives the only honest answer: “O Lord GOD, you know.” Then he is told to prophesy, and the bones come together, bone to its bone, with sinews, flesh and skin; and when the breath comes into them, “they lived, and stood on their feet, a vast multitude.” God explains the vision: “I am going to open your graves, and bring you up from your graves, O my people”; “I will put my spirit within you, and you shall live.” Sirach sings the praises of the ancestors, the famous and the forgotten. “But of others there is no memory”, he admits; yet “these also were godly men, whose righteous deeds have not been forgotten.” “Their bodies are buried in peace, but their name lives on generation after generation.” Most of our grandparents and great-grandparents have no monument but a cross in the parish cemetery. God has not forgotten one of them.

Paul tells the Corinthians what kind of body will rise. As a seed is buried and comes up as a plant, so “What is sown is perishable, what is raised is imperishable. It is sown in dishonor, it is raised in glory. It is sown in weakness, it is raised in power.” We bury our dead with the sign of the cross and with candles, because we sow them like seed in hope: “Just as we have borne the image of the man of dust, we will also bear the image of the man of heaven.” The Gospel shows the judgment that awaits every life. The King gathers the nations and says to those on his right, “Come, you that are blessed by my Father, inherit the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world”, because they fed the hungry, welcomed the stranger, clothed the naked, cared for the sick and visited the prisoner: “just as you did it to one of the least of these who are members of my family, you did it to me.” The Church believes that those who die in God's grace but still need purification are cleansed before they enter the joy of heaven, and that our prayers, our alms and above all the Holy Qurbana offered for them help them. Praying for the dead is itself a work of mercy. So today we pray the oppees at the graves of our dear ones, and we prepare for the Great Fast by remembering that we too are dust, and that we too are sown for glory.
outline: Opening
Ask: whose grave do you visit, and whom do you pray for by name?
Point 1 · Can these bones live?
God opens the graves and gives his Spirit.
Point 2 · Their name lives on
The remembered and the forgotten ancestors.
Point 3 · Sown in weakness, raised in power
The resurrection of the body.
Point 4 · You did it to me
The judgment of love, and the mercy of praying for the dead.
Take-home line
“It is sown in dishonor, it is raised in glory.”
live: Pray for your dead by name
Write down the names of your departed family members and pray for each one today, or have a Holy Qurbana offered for them.
Visit a grave
Visit the parish cemetery this week, light a candle and pray; remember also those whose graves no one visits.
2027-02-05.prayer: Lord Jesus Christ, resurrection and life, you opened the graves of your people and breathed your Spirit into dry bones. Have mercy on all our departed brothers and sisters, our parents, grandparents and ancestors, and all who have no one to pray for them. Purify them and bring them into the joy of your kingdom. Teach us to serve you in the least of your brothers and sisters, so that on the last day we too may hear: come, you that are blessed by my Father. Amen.
altar: The Holy Qurbana is the greatest prayer for the dead: the sacrifice of Christ, offered for the living and the departed, unites the Church on earth with those who await the full vision of God.

2027-02-06.title: Fifth Saturday of Denha
2027-02-06.readTitle: Readings of the day (First Set; mapped from the official calendar, verify locally)
readings: I am standing at the door, knocking
2027-02-06.alt: Season of Denha. Last day of the Season of Denha. Tomorrow is the First Sunday of the Great Fast (Sauma Ramba); the fast itself begins on Monday.
2027-02-06.verse: Listen! I am standing at the door, knocking; if you hear my voice and open the door, I will come in to you and eat with you, and you with me.
theo: The last of the seven letters in Revelation is written to Laodicea, a rich banking city, proud of its textiles and its famous eye-salve, whose water came by aqueduct and arrived lukewarm. The risen Christ, “the Amen, the faithful and true witness”, speaks to it bluntly: “I know your works; you are neither cold nor hot. I wish that you were either cold or hot. So, because you are lukewarm, and neither cold nor hot, I am about to spit you out of my mouth.” Their real sickness is self-satisfaction: “For you say, ‘I am rich, I have prospered, and I need nothing.’ You do not realize that you are wretched, pitiable, poor, blind, and naked.” So he offers them what they think they already have: gold refined by fire, white robes, salve for their eyes. His harshness is love: “I reprove and discipline those whom I love. Be earnest, therefore, and repent.” And then the gentlest words in the whole book: “Listen! I am standing at the door, knocking; if you hear my voice and open the door, I will come in to you and eat with you, and you with me.” The Lord does not break the door down. He knocks, and he waits.

The last Gospel of Denha is a picture of the opposite of Laodicea. Jesus goes up a mountain by the Sea of Galilee and sits down. Great crowds come, “bringing with them the lame, the maimed, the blind, the mute, and many others. They put them at his feet, and he cured them.” These people do not say, I need nothing. They lay their poverty at his feet, and the crowd is amazed “when they saw the mute speaking, the maimed whole, the lame walking, and the blind seeing. And they praised the God of Israel.” Through these weeks of Denha Christ has been revealed: at the Jordan, at Cana, to the first disciples, to Nicodemus, to the Samaritans, to the sick. Tomorrow the Great Fast begins. It is not a season for the self-satisfied, but for those who admit that they are poor and blind, open the door to the one who knocks, and let themselves be carried to his feet.
outline: Opening
Ask: is your faith hot, cold, or lukewarm?
Point 1 · Neither cold nor hot
The danger of saying: I need nothing.
Point 2 · Gold, white robes, salve
What only Christ can give.
Point 3 · I stand at the door
He knocks and waits; he wants to eat with us.
Point 4 · At his feet
The crowd that brought its poverty to Jesus.
Take-home line
“I am standing at the door, knocking.”
live: Open the door (Revelation 3:20)
Before the Great Fast begins, make a good confession or plan when you will make it.
Bring someone to his feet
Pray today for one sick or disabled person by name, and visit or call them if you can.
2027-02-06.prayer: Lord Jesus Christ, faithful and true witness, you stand at the door of our hearts and knock. Forgive our lukewarmness and our pride that says we need nothing. Clothe us in white, anoint our eyes to see, and as the Great Fast begins, let us lay all our poverty at your feet and open the door to you, so that you may come in and eat with us. Amen.
altar: At every Holy Qurbana the promise of Revelation is fulfilled: the Lord comes in and eats with us, and we with him.

2027-02-08.title: First Monday of the Great Fast · Vibhoodi (Ash Monday)
2027-02-08.readTitle: Readings of the day (First Set; mapped from the official calendar, verify locally)
readings: The sin of humanity and its consequence
2027-02-08.alt: Season of the Great Fast (Sauma Ramba). Day of the penitential service (Vibhoodi), with fasting and abstinence from meat.
2027-02-08.verse: leave your gift there before the altar and go; first be reconciled to your brother or sister, and then come and offer your gift.
theo: The Great Fast has begun. Yesterday was Pethurtha Sunday; the Syriac word means putting an end, turning back, and the calendar explains that the days of rich food and celebration are over. In many Syro-Malabar homes Pethurtha evening is still a family meal shared with some solemnity, a farewell to meat and fish until Easter, and in older Syrian Christian households the vessels used for meat were scrubbed clean or set aside for the whole season. The St Thomas Christians have long called this season the fifty days fast, counted from Pethurtha to Easter. Today, the first Monday, the Church keeps the penitential service called Vibhoodi. The ashes are traditionally made by burning the tender coconut-leaf palms kept from last year's Oshana, and the priest traces a cross with them on our foreheads, recalling the word spoken to Adam: “you are dust, and to dust you shall return.” The calendar asks for fasting and abstinence from meat today, and recommends abstinence throughout the season.

It is striking that the Church opens the Great Fast with the first page of the Bible. “In the beginning when God created the heavens and the earth, the earth was a formless void and darkness covered the face of the deep.” Into that darkness God speaks: “Let there be light”; and there was light. Again and again the refrain returns: “God saw that it was good.” The fast is not contempt for the body or for the good things of the world; it is God's word speaking again over the void and darkness in us, bringing order and light. Joshua stands where we stand today, at the edge of a river. Moses is dead, the Jordan lies ahead, and God says: “Be strong and courageous; do not be frightened or dismayed, for the LORD your God is with you wherever you go.” He gives Joshua one method for the crossing: “This book of the law shall not depart out of your mouth; you shall meditate on it day and night.” Paul names what went wrong with humanity: people “exchanged the truth about God for a lie and worshiped and served the creature rather than the Creator.” Fasting puts the creature back in its place, so that the Creator may be first again. And Paul is not ashamed: the gospel “is the power of God for salvation to everyone who has faith.”

In the Gospel Jesus says he has come “not to abolish but to fulfill” the law, and he carries it into the heart. Not only murder, but anger and insult are judged. Then he describes a scene every Christian knows: “So when you are offering your gift at the altar, if you remember that your brother or sister has something against you, leave your gift there before the altar and go; first be reconciled to your brother or sister, and then come and offer your gift.” This is why the Vibhoodi is a penitential service of reconciliation. Ash on the forehead and peace in the home belong together. A fast that gives up fish and meat but keeps a quarrel alive has missed the heart of the matter. Seven weeks lie ahead: dust that knows it is dust, light that God speaks into the dark, courage for the crossing, and a brother or sister waiting for our first step.
outline: Opening
Ask: what does the ash on your forehead say to you this morning?
Point 1 · Remember you are dust
Vibhoodi and the fifty days fast.
Point 2 · Let there be light
The fast as God's new creation in us.
Point 3 · Be strong and courageous
Joshua at the Jordan; the word day and night.
Point 4 · First be reconciled
The gift left before the altar.
Take-home line
“first be reconciled to your brother or sister, and then come and offer your gift.”
live: Fix your fast
Decide today, with your family, what you will give up for the whole Great Fast, and what the saving will be given to.
First be reconciled (Matthew 5:24)
Call, visit or write to one person who has something against you, before Sunday.
Day and night (Joshua 1:8)
Read one chapter of a Gospel every day of the Great Fast.
2027-02-08.prayer: Lord Jesus Christ, at the beginning of this holy fast you mark us with ashes and remind us that we are dust. Speak your light into our darkness, give us courage for the crossing of these days, and do not let us bring our gift to your altar while a brother or sister waits for our pardon. Make this Great Fast a time of new creation for us and for our families. Glory to you, with the Father and the Holy Spirit, for ever. Amen.
altar: Before the Holy Qurbana we make peace with one another; Jesus asks that our gift at the altar come from a reconciled heart.

2027-02-09.title: First Tuesday of the Great Fast
2027-02-09.readTitle: Readings of the day (First Set; mapped from the official calendar, verify locally)
2027-02-09.alt: Season of the Great Fast (Sauma Ramba).
2027-02-09.verse: Or do you despise the riches of his kindness and forbearance and patience? Do you not realize that God's kindness is meant to lead you to repentance?
theo: Yesterday the ash reminded us that we are dust. Today Genesis shows what God does with dust. On the sixth day God says, “Let us make humankind in our image, according to our likeness”, and “God created humankind in his image, in the image of God he created them; male and female he created them.” Then he looks at everything he has made, “and indeed, it was very good.” The second account is more intimate: “then the Lord God formed man from the dust of the ground, and breathed into his nostrils the breath of life; and the man became a living being.” The Great Fast holds both truths together: we are dust, and we carry God's breath and God's image. Fasting is not a punishment of the body; it is the body joining the soul in prayer, so that the image of God may shine more clearly in us. At the edge of the Jordan the people give Joshua an answer worth making our own for these seven weeks: “All that you have commanded us we will do, and wherever you send us we will go.”

Paul turns to those who are quick to condemn: “Therefore you have no excuse, whoever you are, when you judge others; for in passing judgment on another you condemn yourself, because you, the judge, are doing the very same things.” Then he asks a gentle and searching question: “Or do you despise the riches of his kindness and forbearance and patience? Do you not realize that God's kindness is meant to lead you to repentance?” Repentance does not begin with fear; it begins when we discover how kind God has been to us. In the Gospel Jesus asks us to pass that kindness on: “if anyone strikes you on the right cheek, turn the other also; and if anyone wants to sue you and take your coat, give your cloak as well; and if anyone forces you to go one mile, go also the second mile. Give to everyone who begs from you.” The second mile is the Lenten mile. In many Kerala homes and parishes, what the fast saves, the price of the fish and meat not bought, is set aside for the poor. A fast without giving would be only a diet; a fast that gives becomes kindness, the same kindness that first led us back to God.
outline: Opening
Ask: when did God's kindness last bring you back to him?
Point 1 · Dust and breath
Made in God's image, from the ground.
Point 2 · Kindness that leads to repentance
Do not despise God's patience.
Point 3 · The second mile
Generosity as the fruit of the fast.
Take-home line
“God's kindness is meant to lead you to repentance.”
live: Count his kindness (Romans 2:4)
Write down ten kindnesses God has shown you this past year, and thank him for each.
Walk the second mile (Matthew 5:41)
Do one thing more than you are asked today, for someone who asks too much of you.
2027-02-09.prayer: Lord Jesus Christ, you formed us from the dust and breathed your life into us, and you are patient with us when we sin. Do not let us despise your kindness, but let it lead us to repentance. Make us generous like you, ready to turn the other cheek and walk the second mile, and let what our fast saves feed the poor. Amen.
altar: At the Holy Qurbana Christ gives us more than we ask: not only bread, but himself. He has walked the second mile for us.

2027-02-10.title: First Wednesday of the Great Fast
2027-02-10.readTitle: Readings of the day (First Set; mapped from the official calendar, verify locally)
readings: Rahab protects the spies of Israel
Salvation is not through the law
2027-02-10.alt: Season of the Great Fast (Sauma Ramba). Latin Catholics begin Lent today with Ash Wednesday.
2027-02-10.verse: But whenever you pray, go into your room and shut the door and pray to your Father who is in secret; and your Father who sees in secret will reward you.
theo: Genesis shows us the first thing in creation that God calls “not good”: “It is not good that the man should be alone; I will make him a helper as his partner.” The man names every animal, but among them “there was not found a helper as his partner.” So God casts him into a deep sleep, takes one of his ribs and builds a woman, and the man wakes to cry out with joy: “This at last is bone of my bones and flesh of my flesh.” Therefore “a man leaves his father and his mother and clings to his wife, and they become one flesh”, and they “were both naked, and were not ashamed.” We do not keep the Great Fast alone. In Kerala it has always been a family fast: the whole household gives up meat and fish together, and the evening family prayer becomes a little longer. The calendar notes that weddings are not celebrated from the beginning of the fast until Easter, so that the joy of the wedding feast may wait for the joy of the Resurrection. In many homes, especially in the last weeks, the Puthen Pana of Arnos Pathiri, the old Malayalam poem on the life and Passion of Christ, is sung or read aloud. Today our Latin Catholic neighbours receive their ashes; the Church in Kerala walks through these weeks together.

In the second reading an outsider becomes a believer. Rahab of Jericho hides Joshua's spies on her roof and confesses what she has heard: “The LORD your God is indeed God in heaven above and on earth below.” She asks for mercy on her household, and the sign of her safety is a crimson cord tied in the window through which she let them down. Matthew later names her among the ancestors of Jesus. Paul says something similar: “it is not the hearers of the law who are righteous in God's sight, but the doers of the law who will be justified.” Even those without the law can “show that what the law requires is written on their hearts”, while those who know the law may fail to live it: “you, then, that teach others, will you not teach yourself?” Jesus applies this to prayer. Do not pray to be seen. “Go into your room and shut the door and pray to your Father who is in secret.” Do not “heap up empty phrases”, “for your Father knows what you need before you ask him.” The Great Fast invites us into that inner room, where no one is watching except the Father who loves us.
outline: Opening
Ask: where is your inner room, the place where you meet God alone?
Point 1 · Not good to be alone
A family fast, a family prayer.
Point 2 · A crimson cord in the window
Rahab's faith; doers, not only hearers.
Point 3 · The inner room
Prayer seen only by the Father.
Take-home line
“Your Father who sees in secret will reward you.”
live: Shut the door (Matthew 6:6)
Spend ten minutes each day of this week in silent prayer, alone, with your phone outside the room.
Pray as a family
Add one Gospel passage or one decade of the Rosary to your evening family prayer for the whole Great Fast.
2027-02-10.prayer: Lord Jesus Christ, you said it is not good for us to be alone, and you gave us families to walk with us. Make our homes places of prayer during this Great Fast. Give us Rahab's faith, make us doers of your word and not hearers only, and lead each of us into the inner room where the Father sees in secret. Amen.
altar: At the Holy Qurbana we pray together as one family, and in the silence after Communion each of us enters the inner room with Christ.

2027-02-11.title: First Thursday of the Great Fast
2027-02-11.readTitle: Readings of the day (First Set; mapped from the official calendar, verify locally)
readings: The sin of our first parents
2027-02-11.alt: Season of the Great Fast (Sauma Ramba). In the Latin calendar 11 February is Our Lady of Lourdes, the World Day of the Sick.
2027-02-11.verse: But strive first for the kingdom of God and his righteousness, and all these things will be given to you as well.
theo: The serpent's first words are a question that twists God's command: “Did God say, ‘You shall not eat from any tree in the garden’?” Then comes the lie: “You will not die; for God knows that when you eat of it your eyes will be opened, and you will be like God, knowing good and evil.” At the root of the first sin is suspicion: the idea that God is holding something back from us, that he is a rival and not a Father. The eyes are opened, but all they see is nakedness and shame. Then, in the evening breeze, God comes looking: “But the Lord God called to the man, and said to him, “Where are you?”” God knows where Adam is. The question is an invitation to come out. Adam answers with fear, “I was afraid, because I was naked; and I hid myself”, and then with blame: “The woman whom you gave to be with me, she gave me fruit from the tree, and I ate.” The woman blames the serpent. Paul draws the conclusion for every human being: “There is no one who is righteous, not even one”, so that “every mouth may be silenced”, for “through the law comes the knowledge of sin.” The Great Fast begins in honesty: to stop hiding and stop blaming, and to answer God's question with the truth.

Joshua's people are about to enter unknown ground. The ark of the covenant goes ahead of them, carried by the priests, “so that you may know the way you should go, for you have not passed this way before.” Joshua tells them: “Sanctify yourselves; for tomorrow the LORD will do wonders among you.” God goes first into the river. In the Gospel Jesus speaks to the anxiety that began in Eden: “do not worry about your life, what you will eat or what you will drink, or about your body, what you will wear.” “Look at the birds of the air; they neither sow nor reap nor gather into barns, and yet your heavenly Father feeds them.” “Consider the lilies of the field.” In a season of fasting these words land differently. We eat less, and discover that the Father still feeds us. Worry is the old suspicion of the garden, the fear that God will not provide. Jesus answers it with an order of priorities: “But strive first for the kingdom of God and his righteousness, and all these things will be given to you as well.” Today, as the Latin Church remembers Our Lady of Lourdes and prays for the sick, let us bring to God the worries of the sick and of those who care for them.
outline: Opening
Ask: what worry woke you up this week?
Point 1 · Where are you?
Suspicion, hiding and blame; God comes looking.
Point 2 · Sanctify yourselves
The ark goes first into the river.
Point 3 · Strive first for the kingdom
The birds, the lilies, and the fast that teaches trust.
Take-home line
“But strive first for the kingdom of God and his righteousness.”
live: Answer his question (Genesis 3:9)
Tonight, before sleeping, answer God honestly: where am I? Plan your Lenten confession.
Hand over one worry (Matthew 6:34)
Write down one worry and leave it before a crucifix or an image of Our Lady.
2027-02-11.prayer: Lord God, you came looking for Adam in the garden and you still call us: where are you? Free us from the suspicion that you are not good, from hiding and from blaming others. Go before us like the ark into the river, teach us through this fast to trust your care, and help us strive first for your kingdom. Comfort the sick and all who are anxious. Amen.
altar: At the Holy Qurbana the Father gives us our daily bread in its fullest sense, the Body of his Son. We need not worry; he provides.

2027-02-12.title: First Friday of the Great Fast
2027-02-12.readTitle: Readings of the day (First Set; mapped from the official calendar, verify locally)
2027-02-12.alt: Season of the Great Fast (Sauma Ramba). Abstinence from meat; fasting is highly recommended on all the Fridays of the Great Fast.
2027-02-12.verse: Then the Lord said to Cain, “Where is your brother Abel?” He said, “I do not know; am I my brother's keeper?”
theo: Yesterday God asked Adam, “Where are you?” Today he asks Cain, “Where is your brother Abel?” Sin that began as distrust of God quickly turns against the brother. Cain and Abel both bring offerings; God regards Abel's, and Cain's face falls. God speaks to him like a father warning a son: “If you do well, will you not be accepted? And if you do not do well, sin is lurking at the door; its desire is for you, but you must master it.” Cain does not master it. He leads his brother into the field and kills him. When God asks where Abel is, Cain answers with a lie and a shrug: “I do not know; am I my brother's keeper?” But the earth cannot keep the secret: “Listen; your brother's blood is crying out to me from the ground!” And yet even here God shows mercy: he puts a mark on Cain “so that no one who came upon him would kill him.” Jesus speaks to the root of Cain's sin, the comparing and judging eye: “Do not judge, so that you may not be judged.” “Why do you see the speck in your neighbor's eye, but do not notice the log in your own eye?” “You hypocrite, first take the log out of your own eye, and then you will see clearly to take the speck out of your neighbor's eye.”

On the Fridays of the Great Fast our parishes walk the Way of the Cross, often in the evening, and many keep a stricter fast. Abel's blood cried from the ground for justice; on the Cross we see another blood, “the sprinkled blood that speaks a better word than the blood of Abel”, the blood that cries for mercy. The second reading shows the Jordan in flood at harvest time. As soon as the feet of the priests carrying the ark touch the edge of the water, the river stands up “in a single heap”, and the whole people crosses on dry ground. Twelve men lift twelve stones from the riverbed, so that when the children ask, “What do those stones mean to you?”, the answer will be told. Paul holds up Abraham as the father of all who believe: “Hoping against hope, he believed.” He knew his body was “already as good as dead” and Sarah was barren, yet “No distrust made him waver concerning the promise of God, but he grew strong in his faith as he gave glory to God, being fully convinced that God was able to do what he had promised.” These words were written for us too, who believe in the God who raised Jesus, “who was handed over to death for our trespasses and was raised for our justification.” Every Friday of the Great Fast walks toward that Friday, and through it to Easter.
outline: Opening
Ask: who is the brother or sister God has placed in your keeping?
Point 1 · Where is your brother?
Sin lurking at the door; Abel's blood cries out.
Point 2 · Hoping against hope
Abraham's faith, and stones from the Jordan.
Point 3 · First the log
The judging eye healed by the Cross.
Take-home line
“Where is your brother Abel?”
live: Walk the Way of the Cross
Join your parish for the Way of the Cross this evening, or pray it at home with your family.
Be your brother's keeper (Genesis 4:9)
Visit or call one relative or neighbour you have neglected, and ask what they need.
2027-02-12.prayer: Lord Jesus Christ, your blood speaks a better word than the blood of Abel. Master the sin that lurks at the door of our hearts, take the log from our eyes, and make us keepers of our brothers and sisters. Give us the faith of Abraham, hoping against hope, and lead us through the waters of these days to your Easter. Amen.
altar: At the Holy Qurbana we receive the Blood of Christ, which does not cry for vengeance like Abel's but for mercy and peace.

2027-02-13.title: First Saturday of the Great Fast
2027-02-13.readTitle: Readings of the day (First Set; mapped from the official calendar, verify locally)
2027-02-13.alt: Season of the Great Fast (Sauma Ramba).
2027-02-13.verse: And forgive us our debts, as we also have forgiven our debtors.
theo: On Thursday Paul left us with every mouth silenced: no one is righteous, not even one. Today he opens a door: “But now, apart from law, the righteousness of God has been disclosed, and is attested by the law and the prophets, the righteousness of God through faith in Jesus Christ for all who believe.” The sentence that follows is one of the most important in the New Testament: “since all have sinned and fall short of the glory of God; they are now justified by his grace as a gift, through the redemption that is in Christ Jesus, whom God put forward as a sacrifice of atonement by his blood, effective through faith.” This matters at the end of the first week of the Great Fast. We do not buy God's favour with our fasting. Grace comes first, freely, through the blood of Christ. Our fasting, prayer and almsgiving are our response to that gift, and grace itself makes them fruitful. Whoever forgets this turns the fast into a ledger of achievements; whoever remembers it fasts with gratitude.

The Gospel gives us the prayer that holds the whole Great Fast together: “Pray then in this way: Our Father in heaven, hallowed be your name. Your kingdom come. Your will be done, on earth as it is in heaven. Give us this day our daily bread. And forgive us our debts, as we also have forgiven our debtors. And do not bring us to the time of trial, but rescue us from the evil one.” The Holy Qurbana of our Church opens with this prayer and returns to it before Communion. Each line is a Lenten programme: God's name first, his kingdom before our plans, bread asked for one day at a time by people who are fasting, forgiveness given and received, and rescue in the time of trial, as Jesus himself was tested in the wilderness. Of all the petitions, Jesus comments on only one: “For if you forgive others their trespasses, your heavenly Father will also forgive you; but if you do not forgive others, neither will your Father forgive your trespasses.” The week that began with the gift left before the altar ends with the same lesson: the forgiven must forgive.
outline: Opening
Ask: which line of the Our Father is hardest for you to pray honestly?
Point 1 · Justified as a gift
All have sinned; grace comes first.
Point 2 · Our Father
The Lord's Prayer as a Lenten programme.
Point 3 · As we forgive
The one petition Jesus explains.
Take-home line
“And forgive us our debts, as we also have forgiven our debtors.”
live: Pray it slowly (Matthew 6:9–13)
Pray the Our Father once today very slowly, pausing a full minute on each petition.
Forgive as you are forgiven (Matthew 6:14)
Name before God one person you forgive, and go to confession this Saturday if you can.
2027-02-13.prayer: Our Father in heaven, all of us have sinned and fallen short of your glory, and you justify us freely by your grace in Christ Jesus. Let us fast with gratitude and not with pride. Hallow your name in us, bring your kingdom, give us today our daily bread, forgive us as we forgive, and rescue us from the evil one. Through Christ our Lord. Amen.
altar: At the Holy Qurbana we pray the Our Father before Communion: forgiven and forgiving, we receive the Bread of life.

quick: Forty days after his birth, Jesus was presented in the Temple with the offering of the poor.
Simeon took him in his arms: my eyes have seen your salvation.
Anna, who prayed and fasted night and day, spoke of him to all who waited.
2027-02-02.action: Pray by name for a religious sister, brother or priest today and thank them.
2027-02-02.question: Am I waiting for the Lord, or have I stopped expecting him?
catechism: Christ, the end of the law.
kidsaint: Two old friends of God who waited many years in the Temple. When Mary and Joseph brought baby Jesus, they knew at once that he was the Saviour! Lesson: God keeps his promises, so we can wait for him with joy.
2027-02-02.special: Mayaltho: the Presentation of the Lord in the Temple. World Day for Consecrated Life.
term: The Syriac name of today's feast, meaning the Entrance: the Lord enters his Temple.

family.explain: When Jesus was forty days old, Mary and Joseph took him to the Temple to give him to God. They were poor, so they brought two little birds. An old man named Simeon took baby Jesus in his arms and said: now I have seen the Saviour!
family.intention: We pray for religious sisters, brothers and priests, especially those from our family and parish.
family.ask: Ask: “How can we give our day to God this week?”

illus: An illustration

In a parish near Pala an old man came to the morning Qurbana every day for over forty years, always kneeling in the same place. When his first great-grandson was baptized, the priest placed the baby in his arms for a moment. The old man was silent, and then said softly the words he had prayed for so long: now you are dismissing your servant in peace. His family says that was the happiest they ever saw him.

pm.open: Lord Jesus, light of the nations, you came to your Temple to meet those who waited for you. Come and meet us now. Amen.
share: They brought him up to Jerusalem to present him to the Lord (Luke 2:22). What do I need to present to God?
My eyes have seen your salvation (Luke 2:30). Where have I seen God's salvation?
She never left the temple but worshiped there with fasting and prayer (Luke 2:37). How faithful am I in prayer?
pm.resp: Lord, our eyes have seen your salvation.
interc: For the Church, that she may be a light to the nations.
For religious sisters, brothers and priests, on this World Day for Consecrated Life.
For young people discerning a vocation.
For the elderly who pray for the Church, like Simeon and Anna.
For mothers and newborn children.
For our group, that we may be ready to meet the Lord.
pm.close: Father, your Son entered his Temple and was received by those who waited for him. Make us watchful and full of hope, and let his light shine through us. Through Christ our Lord. Amen.

quick: Moses fasted forty days with God, and his face shone.
God's chosen fast is justice and sharing bread with the hungry.
Jesus overcame the tempter with the word of God: one does not live by bread alone.
2027-02-07.action: At Pethurtha tonight, ask pardon of one family member and forgive one person.
2027-02-07.question: What will make this Great Fast different from last year's?
kidsaint: He stayed on the mountain with God for forty days. When he came down, his face was shining with God's light, and he did not even know it! Lesson: when we spend time with God, his light shines through us.
2027-02-07.special: First Sunday of the Great Fast. Pethurtha. The Great Fast begins tomorrow.
term: The Syriac name of the Great Fast: the fifty days of prayer, fasting and almsgiving before the Pasha of the Lord.

family.explain: Jesus went into the desert and did not eat for forty days. When he was very hungry, the devil said: make bread from these stones! Jesus said no: God's word is more important than bread. In the Great Fast we give up some things to grow closer to God.
family.intention: We pray for a holy Great Fast for our family and our parish.
family.ask: Ask: “What will each of us give up, and what will we give to the poor, in this Great Fast?”

illus: An illustration

In a family in Kuravilangad the grandmother used to keep a small wooden box on the prayer table during the Great Fast. Every time someone in the house gave up a snack, a tea at the shop or a cinema ticket, the money went into the box. At Easter the children carried it to a home for the elderly nearby. Her grandson, now grown up, says that he forgot most of the sermons of his childhood, but never that box.

pm.open: Lord Jesus, led by the Spirit into the desert, lead us into this Great Fast with you. Amen.
share: He was there with the LORD forty days and forty nights (Exodus 34:28). How will I spend more time with God in these fifty days?
Is not this the fast that I choose? (Isaiah 58:6). What injustice or quarrel must I put right?
One does not live by bread alone (Matthew 4:4). What word of God will I feed on?
pm.resp: Lord, teach us to fast as you fasted.
interc: For the whole Church as she begins the Great Fast.
For those who are tempted and those who have fallen.
For the hungry, the homeless and workers who are oppressed.
For families, that they may be reconciled at Pethurtha.
For our group, that we may put on the new self.
pm.close: Father, your Son overcame the tempter by your word. Strengthen us through these fifty days, and bring us renewed to the joy of his Resurrection. Through Christ our Lord. Amen.

quick: Enoch walked with God in an ordinary home: that is the goal of the fast.
Our Lenten customs are stones that tell our children the story of Christ.
Hear the word and do it: build your house on the rock.
2027-02-14.action: Choose one teaching of Jesus from Matthew 5–7 and live it every day this week.
2027-02-14.question: Am I only hearing the word, or also doing it?
kidsaint: They were two brothers from Thessalonica who went to the Slav peoples. They made an alphabet for their language, so that the people could read the Bible and pray the liturgy in their own words. Lesson: God wants everyone to hear his word and live it!
2027-02-14.special: Second Sunday of the Great Fast.
term: Syriac for the Great Fast: the seven weeks of prayer, fasting and almsgiving that prepare the Church for the Passion and Resurrection of Christ.

family.explain: Jesus told a story about two men who built houses. One built on rock, the other on sand. When the big rain and floods came, the house on sand fell down, but the house on rock stood strong. Jesus says: whoever listens to my words and does them is like the man who built on rock.
family.intention: We pray for families who have lost their homes, and for all who face storms in life.
family.ask: Ask: “What is one thing Jesus says that we can do together this week?”

illus: An illustration

When floodwater rose around a village near Chengannur, an old house built by a grandfather on a high stone plinth stood firm while several newer houses nearby were badly damaged. Long before, the grandfather had insisted on digging down to hard laterite, though the neighbours laughed at the cost and the delay. His grandson, now a catechist, tells his class every Lent: hearing the word is drawing the plan; doing it is the digging. The flood does not ask which house was prettier.

pm.open: Lord Jesus, rock of our salvation, we gather to hear your words. Help us to do them. Amen.
share: Enoch walked with God (Genesis 5:24). What would it mean for me to walk with God this week?
What do these stones mean? (Joshua 4:21). How do I explain my faith to the next generation?
Everyone who hears these words of mine and acts on them (Matthew 7:24). Which word of Jesus am I hearing but not doing?
pm.resp: Lord, build our house on the rock.
interc: For the Church, that she may hear and do the word of God.
For families who have lost their homes in floods and disasters.
For parents and grandparents, that they may hand on the faith.
For catechumens preparing for baptism.
For our group, that our faith may stand in every storm.
pm.close: Father, you call us not only to say Lord, Lord, but to do your will. Build our lives on Christ the rock, and make our families walk with you. Through Christ our Lord. Amen.

quick: The Lord is faithful even when not all have faith.
A woman touched his cloak and was made well: take heart, daughter.
Jesus took the dead girl by the hand and she got up.
2027-02-01.action: Pray by name for one missionary or catechist today.
2027-02-01.question: Do I trust more in my own faith or in the Lord's faithfulness?

family.explain: A sick woman thought: if I only touch Jesus' clothes, I will be well. She touched him and she was healed! Then Jesus went to a house where a little girl had died. He took her hand, and she got up!
family.intention: We pray for sick children and for all who are waiting for healing.
family.ask: Ask: “What can we bring to Jesus today, the way the woman reached out to him?”

illus: An illustration

A nurse at a hospital in Kottayam used to notice an old woman who came every evening to sit beside her husband in the intensive care unit. She said little, but each evening she touched the small crucifix on her rosary and then touched her husband's hand. When the nurse asked her once if she was not tired, she said: my faith is very small, but the Lord is faithful; I only have to reach out.

pm.open: Lord Jesus, faithful and true, we reach out to touch you. Turn to us and heal us. Amen.
share: The Lord is faithful (2 Thessalonians 3:3). Where have I seen his faithfulness in my life?
If I only touch his cloak, I will be made well (Matthew 9:21). What do I want to bring to him?
He took her by the hand, and the girl got up (Matthew 9:25). Whom do I want him to raise up?
pm.resp: Lord, you are faithful; strengthen us.
interc: For the spread of the word of the Lord in our land.
For the sick, especially those suffering for many years.
For parents who grieve for their children.
For those who feel shut out and unclean.
For our group, that our hearts may be directed to the love of God.
pm.close: Father, your Son turned to the woman who reached out and raised the girl who had died. Strengthen our faith and guard us from the evil one. Through Christ our Lord. Amen.

quick: Paul: proclaim the message, whether the time is favourable or unfavourable.
The Samaritan woman left her water jar and brought her town to Jesus.
Jesus: my food is to do the will of him who sent me.
2027-02-03.action: Thank God today by name for the person who first taught you the faith.
2027-02-03.question: What feeds me more: my own wishes or the will of God?

family.explain: A woman met Jesus at a well. She was so happy that she forgot her water jar and ran into town shouting: come and see! Many people came to meet Jesus because of her.
family.intention: We pray for catechism teachers and all who teach the faith to children.
family.ask: Ask: “Who taught us about Jesus, and how can we thank them?”

illus: An illustration

A catechism teacher in a parish near Thodupuzha taught the Sunday class for nearly forty years. Many of her pupils drifted away, and she sometimes wondered if her work had borne any fruit. In her old age one of those pupils, now a priest, came back to celebrate a Holy Qurbana in the parish. In his homily he said: she sowed, and I am only reaping. She sat in the front row, crying.

pm.open: Lord Jesus, you are the living water. Fill us, so that we too may leave our jars and run to tell others. Amen.
share: Proclaim the message; be persistent whether the time is favorable or unfavorable (2 Timothy 4:2). Where am I called to speak about Christ?
She left her water jar (John 4:28). What must I leave to follow Jesus?
My food is to do the will of him who sent me (John 4:34). What is God's will for me this week?
pm.resp: Lord, may your will be our food.
interc: For preachers, catechists and missionaries.
For those who have itching ears and turn away from the truth.
For outsiders who are waiting to hear about Christ.
For those who first taught us the faith, living and departed.
For our group, that we may do the Father's will.
pm.close: Father, your Son found his food in doing your will. Send us into the harvest and give us joy in the work. Through Christ our Lord. Amen.

quick: Peter: regard the patience of our Lord as salvation.
Jesus: do not judge; first take the log out of your own eye.
St John de Britto became all things to all people and died for Christ in Tamil Nadu.
2027-02-04.action: Before criticizing anyone today, name one fault of your own and ask God's pardon.
2027-02-04.question: Do I measure others with the patience God shows me?

family.explain: Jesus told a funny picture-story: a man with a big log in his own eye tries to take a tiny speck out of his friend's eye! Jesus means: before we find fault with others, let us look at our own faults.
family.intention: We pray for missionaries, through St John de Britto.
family.ask: Ask: “Can we go one whole day this week without finding fault with anyone?”

illus: An illustration

A Syro-Malabar family from Kerala, working in Chennai, visited the shrine of St John de Britto at Oriyur. The father, who was quick to criticize his Tamil neighbours, read on a board how Arul Anandar had learned their language, worn their dress and eaten their food in order to love them. On the way home he said quietly: I have lived among them ten years and never learned to greet them in their own tongue. The next week he began to learn Tamil from the neighbour's son.

pm.open: Lord Jesus, merciful and patient, take the logs from our eyes so that we may see clearly. Amen.
share: Regard the patience of our Lord as salvation (2 Peter 3:15). How has God been patient with me?
Do not judge, and you will not be judged (Luke 6:37). Whom have I been judging?
